cells.tense: You are in it right now, and the practice is moving under its own weight.
cells.ask: Add one small repeat to something you already do — same time tomorrow, a hand's worth of effort. Keep the rest as it is.
cells.core:
The practice has stopped needing to be pushed. You sit down with it, it moves, you get up, and the skill gets a little finer in the process. It isn't dramatic from the inside. It doesn't need to be.

Being alone in it has quit being a hiding place. You go in and come back with more of yourself, and people catch the difference even when they don't know where it's from. Refining this is feeding something. It isn't covering for a fear that stop working and it all falls down. There's room in the routine as it stands. Keep the practice close, keep it small, and let Breakthrough do its work when a structure has already done its job and is ready to come down.
cells.sheetLine: The practice carries itself now, and you are in the room with it.
cells.verb: keeping a small practice alive by returning to it

cells.tense: You are practising for a day that has not arrived, and it is costing you the day you have.
cells.ask: Pick the smallest piece of the practice and do only that today — five minutes, no checking it after. Leave the rest for tomorrow.
cells.core:
The practising has turned into staying ahead of a judgment that hasn't come. One more pass, one more session, one more version — there's a finish line out in front and it keeps moving, so you keep going and the going doesn't land.

Solitude you once chose is now the only place that feels safe, which is a different thing. Stop and it all slides, so you don't stop. That fear is doing the scheduling.

Picture the version where the practice gives instead of guards: small, repeated, and over when it's over. A session can end like an ending rather than a defeat. Letting one thing be finished is the release Faith runs on, and it doesn't take the skill with it.
cells.sheetLine: You are practising for a verdict that hasn't arrived yet.
cells.verb: keeping a small practice alive by returning to it

cells.tense: You set the practice down a while back, and picking it up again is the part that won't happen.
cells.ask: Do one session so short it isn't worth counting — a few minutes, badly, alone. Set a timer and stop when it goes.
cells.core:
There's something you'd like to be able to do through repetition, and you can't get a run at it. A few days, then nothing. Dropping it that fast isn't laziness exactly. It arrives like a door already behind you, and your body keeps acting as if it's shut.

Meanwhile people can offer you things — instruction, company — and it doesn't seem to take. What's thin isn't the want. It's the ordinary back-and-forth where you put in a little and something comes back.

Start with what's fair rather than what's ambitious. A couple of minutes is a real session. Do one, stop on purpose, and let what you put in and get back run in amounts that fit the day. That is how a practice gets a floor under it again.
cells.sheetLine: You can't get a run at it, and starting feels like the locked door.
cells.verb: keeping a small practice alive by returning to it

cells.tense: The practising is happening now, and you would not call it that if asked.
cells.ask: Take one thing you did today and write down when you did it last — one line, just the times. No decision attached.
cells.core:
You get better at things without noticing you're doing it. The repetitions are already running — the same route, the same drills, the same hour set aside — but they show up in your account of yourself as your nature, or as nothing at all. Skill keeps arriving as if it cost nothing.

That isn't magic and it isn't luck. It's attention, spent steadily, over a long time.

Picture the same routine carried on with a bit more give in it. Refining because it's interesting, not because the next version has to be closer to perfect. Start by saying what you actually did and when, once, in your own record. Ambiguity doesn't need to be resolved for the next step to be taken. Claiming the practice is the step.
cells.sheetLine: You keep getting better at this and calling it nothing.
cells.verb: keeping a small practice alive by returning to it

attempts.check: The record supports a small steady practice as the core capacity, but it does not say what earlier practice felt like; in the Too Little cell I locate the person at a door without naming the room behind it, so nothing about what happened there is claimed. The likely objection is to the Unacknowledged cell — a person may say they genuinely don't practise anything, but what the cell describes is the practising happening without being owned, so the ask still lands either way. The ask is a single first session done badly or for a few minutes, doable without anyone's help, and if the read is wrong the person still ends the day having tried something. The sentence that serves me more than them is any reframe that turns bracing toward a practice into devotion to a practice; I have cut that figure and left the plain description instead.

attempts.check: The record supports a small steady practice as the capacity, but says nothing about what earlier practice felt like; the Too Little cell stays at the shape of the falling-off without naming what happened or who was there. The likely objection is to the Unacknowledged cell — someone may say they simply don't practice — but the cell describes repetition already running under a reason they'd give instead, and the showing-up keeps landing either way. The ask is one short, private act with a built-in ending, doable without money or a person, and it survives the read being wrong because it costs a few minutes and teaches what the person actually does. The sentence that serves me more than them is a tidy figure turning a lost routine into a locked room; that image is gone and the plain description stands.
